newsitem.title: HONG KONG: East Timor's Horta says U.N. peace talks "a farce".
newsitem.headline: East Timor's Horta says U.N. peace talks "a farce".

text.p: East Timor's 1996 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Jose Ramos-Horta said on Tuesday Portugal had postponed a round of U.N.-brokered peace talks with Indonesia last month over East Timor because the process was "a farce".

He said the ninth round of U.N. talks between Portugal, regarded as East Timor's administering power, and Indonesia, which has ruled the territory since a 1975 invasion, was postponed by Lisbon last month with his backing.

"The ninth round of talks between Indonesia and Portugal was postponed by the Secretary-General, but (it was) because Portugal took the right stand in refusing to go on to talks....because politically it was untenable for Portugal to continue the talks with Indonesia without any result.
"The eighth round of talks in June... was an embarrassment, a farce. After eight rounds the secretary general's talks produced nothing," he told the Foreign Correspondents' Club in Hong Kong.
Portugal and Indonesia have met periodically under the auspices of the United Nations over the future of East Timor.
The United Nations does not recognise Jakarta's rule over the half-island 500 km (300 miles) north of Australia.

Relations between Lisbon and Jakarta sank to new lows after the award of the Nobel Peace Prize to East Timor's Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo and exiled resistance spokesman Ramos-Horta three months ago.

The United Nations attributed postponement of the December 21 meeting to it coinciding with Boutros Boutros-Ghali's replacement as U.N. secretary-general by Kofi Annan, and to the "need for more preparation".
Portugal has proposed the next round of talks, for which no date have been set, should be preceded by preliminary meetings between the two countries' ambassadors to the United Nations.

Ramos-Horta said the new secretary-general Annan should be given time to explore the issue, but warned he had asked Portugal to press the Security Council to take up the issue of East Timor again if no serious progress was made.
"There is a new secretary-general, Kofi Annan, a man of integrity and experience. We all should give him a chance to explore new ideas," he said.
Annan said on his appointment in December that he would look "very critically" at the United Nations' role in regard to East Timor.

This week, while visiting Macau, Ramos-Horta said the transitions of the British colony of Hong Kong and Portuguese-governed Macau to Chinese rule in 1997 and 1999 provided a possible model for a political solution in East Timor.
Ramos-Horta said he scrapped plans to visit the Philippines because Manila, apparently keen not to antagonise Southeast Asian neighbour Indonesia, had for a third time denied him a visa.
